pages.name: One rule, many pairs
pages.text: Put any x into `y = 2x + 1` to get its y, and that pair fits the rule: (0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 5) and endless more. Plotted, they make one straight line, line 1. The test point's readout ticks only when it sits on that line.

pages.alt: A squared grid, x from 0 to 8 and y from 0 to 14. Line 1, solid: y = 2x + 1. The test point is at (3, 7), fitting the rule.

pages.name: How many pairs?
pages.task: How many pairs of numbers (x, y) fit the rule `x + y = 7`? Drag the test point to try some.
pages.why: Any two numbers that add to 7 fit, such as (3, 4), (2, 5) and (2.5, 4.5), and there are endless more. Plotted, they fill one straight line.

pages.name: A second rule
pages.text: Line 2, dashed, holds every pair that fits `x + y = 7`, such as (0, 7), (3, 4) and (7, 0). At `x = 0` the lines are 6 apart, and each 1 along line 1 climbs 2 while line 2 drops 1, so the gap shuts by `2 − (−1) = 3` and they meet once, at the [[crossing point]] (2, 5). That pair fits both rules at once: it is the [[solution]] of these two [[simultaneous equations]], which means true at the same time.

pages.name: Fits both?
pages.task: Which pair makes `y = 2x + 1` and `x + y = 7` both true?
pages.why: The pair must fit both rules, and (2, 5) does: `2 × 2 + 1 = 5` and `2 + 5 = 7`. (3, 7) fits line 1 only, and (3, 4) fits line 2 only.

pages.name: Turn line 2
pages.text: Turn line 2 with its m handle and the crossing moves. At `y = x + 7` the lines meet at (6, 13). At `y = 1.5x + 7` the gap of 6 shuts by only 0.5 each 1 along, so they meet at `x = 12`, off the grid but still there.

pages.name: Off the grid
pages.why: At `x = 0` line 2 is 6 above line 1, and line 1 climbs `2 − 1.8 = 0.2` more for each 1 along, so the gap shuts at `x = 6 ÷ 0.2 = 30`. There both rules give 61: `2 × 30 + 1 = 61` and `1.8 × 30 + 7 = 61`.

pages.name: Same m
pages.why: Both rules have `m = 3`, so the lines have the same tilt. At every x the first is `2 − (−4) = 6` above the second, so the gap never closes. The lines are parallel, and no pair fits both.

pages.alt: A squared grid, x from 0 to 8 and y from 0 to 14. Line 1, solid: y = 3x + 2. Line 2, dashed: y = 3x minus  4. The lines are parallel.

pages.name: Same line
pages.text: Here line 2 is `2y = 4x + 2`. Halve every term and it is `y = 2x + 1`, line 1 again, so the dashed line lies on top of the solid one. Every point on it fits both rules, so there are endless solutions.

pages.name: Endless solutions
pages.task: Which rule, with `y = 2x + 1`, has endless solutions?
pages.why: Add `2x` to both sides of `y − 2x = 1` and it is `y = 2x + 1`, the same line, so every pair on it fits both. `y = 2x + 3` runs parallel, 2 above, and `y = x + 2` crosses line 1 once, at (1, 3).

pages.name: A reading
pages.text: Here line 2 is `x + y = 5`, and the grid zooms in to tenths. The lines cross between the tenths, so the nearest the test point gets, (1.3, 3.7), fits line 2 but gives `2 × 1.3 + 1 = 3.6` on line 1. A reading from a graph is an [[estimate]], so put it back into both rules to check; the readout's gap sum is exact, `x = 4/3`, and the next two lessons turn it into a method for any pair of equations.
